answers.answer:
### Where caps are (2025-2026 data)
The best countywide figure is **Matthews' H1 2026 average of 5.37%**, built from 11 trades totaling about $199M. Matthews' Q3 2025 report said caps "held near 5.0%." For Q1 2026, Colliers reported a Tri-County range running from 4.02% in Pismo Beach up to **5.79% in Ventura**, the high end of the region. Ventura County therefore trades at a yield premium to Santa Barbara and SLO.

| Segment | Working range | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Countywide average | 5.0%-5.4% | Matthews Q3 2025 (~5.0%), H1 2026 (5.37%) |
| Class A, post-2010, 100+ units | ~4.75%-5.25% (est.) | Unleveraged BlackRock buy of 2023-built Santal (Oct 2025) |
| 1970s-1990s garden, 100+ units | ~5.0%-5.5% (est.) | Cypress Point (1990), Allure, FPA Conejo buys |
| 5-32 units, older | 5.0%-5.75% | LAAA closings: Ventura 8u at 5.02% (2024), Oxnard 18u at 5.47% (2025), Ojai 32u at 5.63% (2025) |
| 2-4 units | ~3.75%-4.75% (est.) | Priced off residential comps, not NOI |

### Submarket and vintage pattern
- **Conejo Valley** (Thousand Oaks, Westlake Village, Oak Park) trades at the lowest caps.
- **Ventura and Camarillo** sit in the middle.
- **Oxnard, Port Hueneme, Santa Paula and Fillmore** usually trade about 25-50 bps higher (estimate).
- Newer vintages command tighter caps. CBRE's Q1 2026 data shows 2010s-built product renting for $2,890 a month, against $2,471 for 1970s-built product.

### So what
Today's caps sit close to the 5.5%-6.25% cost of permanent debt that Colliers reported in mid-2026, so most buyers get little or no positive leverage. Pitch sellers on value at a 5.0%-5.5% going-in cap, not the 4% caps of 2021-2022. With only 11 trades in the H1 sample, one large deal can move the average.
keyPoints: Matthews H1 2026 countywide average cap rate: 5.37% (11 trades, ~$199M)
Colliers Q1 2026 Tri-County range: 4.02% (Pismo Beach) to 5.79% (Ventura)
LAAA small-deal closings: 5.02% (Ventura 8u), 5.47% (Oxnard 18u), 5.63% (Ojai 32u)
Conejo Valley trades tightest; Oxnard and the Santa Clara River Valley trade highest
Permanent debt at 5.5%-6.25% (mid-2026) means little or no positive leverage at a 5.4% cap

answers.summary: The countywide average GRM is about 11.4x. Matthews' H1 2026 figure was 11.44, down from about 15.6x in 2022. Oxnard-area product generally trades around 10-12x, and the Conejo Valley and Ojai at 12-14x.
answers.answer:
### The data
| Period | Avg GRM (Ventura County) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 15.56 | Matthews |
| 2023 | 13.90 | Matthews |
| H1 2026 | 11.44 | Matthews |

GRMs have compressed about 4 turns since 2022. Two forces drove it: prices stopped rising as rates went up, and rents kept climbing (Matthews puts rent growth at more than 15% over five years). The result is that a buyer now pays less for each dollar of gross rent.

### By submarket (working ranges, estimated)
- **Oxnard, Port Hueneme, Santa Paula, Fillmore:** ~10-12x
- **Ventura, Camarillo, Simi Valley, Moorpark:** ~11-13x
- **Thousand Oaks, Westlake Village, Oak Park, Ojai, beach-adjacent Ventura:** ~12-14x+
- **2-4 units:** often 14-17x, because they are priced off home values rather than rent

### Reading a GRM
GRM = price / gross scheduled annual rent. It ignores expenses, so use it as a quick screen, not for valuation. A quick conversion: if NOI is about 60% of gross rent after vacancy and a 35%-40% expense load, then **cap rate is roughly 0.60 / GRM**. At 11.44x that works out to about 5.2%, which is consistent with the reported 5.37% average cap.

### So what
- A **high GRM with a low cap rate** usually means one of two things: rents are well below market, or expenses are heavy (old systems, owner-paid utilities, high property tax after a recent sale).
- In a listing pitch, show both metrics. Sellers anchored on 2021-2022 trades tend to remember 15-16x and will overprice.
keyPoints: GRM = price / gross annual rent and ignores expenses
Rule of thumb: cap rate ≈ 0.60 / GRM, so 11.44x ≈ 5.2%
Oxnard area ~10-12x; Conejo Valley and Ojai ~12-14x (estimate)
2-4 units trade at higher GRMs because they are priced off residential comps

answers.summary: Ventura County cap rates have expanded about 100-120 bps since 2022, from roughly 4.2% to roughly 5.4%. GRMs fell from about 15.6x to about 11.4x. Rent growth has cushioned the hit to per-unit values.
answers.answer:
### The path
| Period | Avg cap rate | Avg GRM | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 4.19% | 15.56 | Matthews (2024 update) |
| 2023 | 4.66% | 13.90 | Matthews (2024 update) |
| Q3 2025 | ~5.0% (narrative) | n/a | Matthews Q3 2025 |
| H1 2026 | 5.37% | 11.44 | Matthews H1 2026 |

That is roughly **+120 bps** from 2022 to H1 2026. The 10-year Treasury, which was under 2% in early 2022, was running 4.4%-4.7% in mid-2026, and Colliers put permanent multifamily debt at 5.5%-6.25%. Caps did not rise as much as rates did, so the spread between cap rate and Treasury yield is now very thin.

### Why prices did not fall as much as caps imply
Rents kept rising. Matthews reports rents up more than 15% over five years, so higher NOI offset part of the cap expansion. Matthews' average price per unit went from **$309,740 in 2022 to $337,287 in 2023**. In H1 2026 it was about $306K, but that sample was weighted toward smaller assets.

### Volume took the real hit
Matthews counted **36 sales in 2022 and 26 in 2023**. In January 2024 it reported zero Q1 sales against 26 listings. Volume came back in 2024, to about $725M per Matthews, and then fell again in 2025.

### 2026 direction
CBRE's H1 2026 survey found cap rates broadly flat nationally, but respondents were most bearish on infill multifamily. Expect Ventura caps to stay roughly level, around 5.0%-5.5%, rather than compress, unless the 10-year moves meaningfully lower.

### So what
A seller who bought, or was appraised, in 2021-2022 at a 4% cap needs to hear the math plainly: holding NOI constant, moving from a 4.2% cap to a 5.4% cap is about a **22% value reduction**. Rent growth has offset part of that.
keyPoints: Net expansion of about 100-120 bps since 2022
GRM compressed from 15.56 to 11.44
Rents up more than 15% over five years (Matthews) partly offset the value hit
Constant NOI from a 4.2% to a 5.4% cap is about a 22% value decline

answers.summary: Deals that close are clearing at about 94-95% of list price, based on 11 MLS-recorded closings in the 12 months to September 2026. Many listings priced off 2021-2022 cap rates don't sell at all. The effective bid-ask gap on unsold listings is about 5-10% of price, or 25-50 bps of cap rate.
answers.answer:
### What the closed data shows
On October 27, 2026 we pulled Flexmls market statistics for Ventura County, multifamily property type, for October 2025 through September 2026. The window had **11 closed sales**:
- **Sale-to-original-list ratio:** about **94.3%** (weighted). Monthly readings ranged from 90.9% to 101%.
- **Sale-to-final-list ratio:** about **95.1%**. Most sellers cut price before going into escrow.

This is a thin sample from one MLS feed, so treat it as directional.

### Where the gap comes from
- **Sellers** remember 4%-4.5% caps and 15x GRMs from 2021-2022. Matthews reports a 4.19% average cap and a 15.56 GRM for 2022.
- **Buyers** need yield close to their cost of debt. Colliers put permanent multifamily debt at **5.5%-6.25%** in mid-2026, and Matthews' H1 2026 average cap was **5.37%**.
- That puts the gap at roughly **25-75 bps of cap rate**, or about 5%-12% of price, on listings that are not trading.

### How it has evolved
The gap was widest in 2023. In January 2024, Matthews counted zero Ventura County sales for the quarter against 26 properties on the market. It narrowed through 2024, which ran about $725M in volume, and again into 2026 as sellers adjusted. Institutional deals such as Tempo ($105M) and Allure ($69.5M) are clearing with competitive bidding.

### So what
- **Price within about 5% of where you expect it to clear.** The data shows closings at roughly 94%-95% of original list, so a 10%-15% cushion is too much.
- **Set expectations in the listing agreement** with a reduction schedule at 30 and 60 days.
- **Anchor on the cap rate.** Buyers underwrite yield, not $/unit.
keyPoints: Flexmls Ventura multifamily, Oct 2025-Sep 2026: 11 closings at ~94.3% of original list and ~95.1% of final list
Gap on unsold listings: ~25-75 bps of cap rate (~5%-12% of price)
Buyers' cost of debt: 5.5%-6.25% (Colliers, mid-2026) against a 5.37% average cap
Peak gap was in 2023: Matthews found 0 sales vs. 26 listings in January 2024
Price within about 5% of the expected clearing level

answers.summary: In the MLS data, Ventura County multifamily listings that sold in the 12 months to September 2026 averaged about 57 days on market, with a range of 16 to 225 days. The prior 12 months averaged about 34 days. Properly priced 5+ unit deals typically reach contract in 30-90 days.
answers.answer:
### Data (Flexmls market statistics, Ventura County, multifamily, pulled 2026-10-27)
| 12 months ending | Closed sales | Avg DOM (weighted) | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sep 2025 | 13 | ~34 days | 1-199 |
| Sep 2026 | 11 | ~57 days | 16-225 |

### Interpreting it
- **DOM has lengthened.** It went from roughly one month to roughly two. That fits a market where buyers underwrite more carefully and sellers come down in steps.
- **The very low readings (1-2.5 days) are telling.** They usually mean the deal was pre-marketed or sold off-market and then entered in the MLS for the record.
- **Outliers like 225 days** are overpriced listings that eventually cut price.
- **DOM resets** when a listing is cancelled and relisted. True market time is often longer than the reported number, so check cumulative DOM and the listing history.

### Commercial-marketed deals
Larger 5+ unit offerings marketed by investment brokers on CoStar/LoopNet, Crexi or a broker's own platform usually follow this rhythm:
- 3-6 weeks of marketing to a call-for-offers date
- 30-60 day escrow, plus a 15-30 day due diligence contingency

That adds up to about **75-120 days from launch to close** (estimate based on typical practice).

### So what
- **Tell sellers to plan on 3-4 months to close.**
- **A listing past 60 DOM without an offer is a pricing problem,** not a marketing problem.
- **Track your competitors' DOM** to find listings that are about to expire. They are good prospecting targets.
keyPoints: Avg DOM, 12 months to Sep 2026: ~57 days (11 MLS sales); prior year ~34 days
Very low DOM (1-3 days) usually signals a pre-marketed or off-market deal recorded in the MLS
DOM resets on relist, so check cumulative DOM and listing history
Typical launch-to-close for a marketed 5+ deal: ~75-120 days
60+ DOM without offers usually means the price is wrong

answers.summary: There is no published expiration rate. MLS data suggests only about 40-50% of multifamily listings sell within a year. In the 12 months to September 2026 there were 24 new listings and 11 sales. Expect about half of listings to expire, be withdrawn, or relist.
answers.answer:
### Proxy from MLS flow (Flexmls, Ventura County, multifamily)
| 12 months ending | New listings | Closed sales | Sales ÷ new listings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sep 2025 | 32 | 13 | ~41% |
| Sep 2026 | 24 | 11 | ~46% |

This is not an exact expiration rate. New listings and closings in a given window come from different cohorts, and relists count as new listings. Still, it points the same way every time: **roughly half or more of listings do not close within the year.** Active inventory held at 3-8 listings a month while sales ran 0-3 a month.

### Supporting evidence
- In January 2024, Matthews counted **26 Ventura County multifamily properties on the market and zero closed sales** that quarter. That was the peak of the bid-ask freeze.
- In the 12 months to September 2026, closings averaged about 94% of original list, so listings that do sell usually needed a price cut. Listings that never cut tend to expire.

### Why listings fail here
1. **Pricing off 2021-2022 caps.** Sellers expect 4%-4.5% caps, but trades are clearing around 5.0%-5.4%.
2. **Below-market rents with AB 1482 limits** on how quickly a buyer can raise them.
3. **Deferred maintenance and SB 721 balcony inspection findings** that turn up in due diligence.
4. **"Testing the market" sellers** with no real motivation.

### So what
- **Expired and withdrawn listings are prime prospecting targets.** The owner has already decided to sell and has just learned the price.
- **Pull the expireds every month** from CRMLS and from CoStar/LoopNet "off market" status, and approach with a pricing analysis.

Prior year: 32 new listings vs. 13 sales (~41%)

### Why the numbers disagree
- **CBRE (MSCI-based)** counts larger deals, roughly $5M and up, so a quarter can show $0.
- **Matthews and CoStar** include smaller trades.
- **Colliers** uses its own Tri-County tally.

Don't splice the series together. Quote one source and name it.

### The story
- **2021-2022:** low rates, peak pricing (4.19% average cap in 2022).
- **2023:** a frozen bid-ask gap.
- **2024:** big portfolio sales, including FPA's $171M and $153M Conejo portfolios, Ranch at Moorpark at $133.2M, and The Landing at Arroyo at $95M.
- **2025:** smaller volume, though it included Cypress Point ($100M) and Santal ($83M).
- **2026:** opened strong with Tempo ($105M) and Allure ($69.5M) in Q1, then went quiet among large deals in Q2.

### So what
A handful of $70M-$170M deals drives the annual totals. The small-building market, where most of your listings will come from, is steadier: roughly 20-40 trades a year.

answers.summary: Turnkey buildings trade at roughly 50-100 bps lower cap rates than comparable value-add product. That is about 10%-20% more per unit, and new construction sits well above both. The premium is narrower than in 2021, because buyers now pay for in-place income rather than upside.
answers.answer:
### Evidence of the spread
- **Vintage rent gap:** CBRE Q1 2026 average rents run **$2,890 for 2010s-built** product against **$2,471 for 1970s-built**, a 17% difference.
- **Price gap:** Santal Thousand Oaks (built 2023) traded at about **$585K per unit**. Older Conejo garden product went at about **$374K per unit** (FPA's 1965-70 Oakview and Biltmore). Smaller older assets countywide averaged about **$270K per unit** in Q2 2026 (Matthews).
- **Current vs. market cap on a value-add listing:** 186 Bell Way in Ventura is marketed at a 4.88% current / 5.88% market cap. The buyer of a value-add building pays today for income that only shows up after renovation and turnover.

### How to think about the premium (working ranges, estimated)
| Condition | Going-in cap | $/unit vs. value-add |
|---|---|---|
| Value-add (original systems, deferred work) | 5.5%-6.0%+ | baseline |
| Clean, updated, no deferred maintenance | 5.0%-5.4% | +10%-20% |
| New construction (post-2015) | ~4.75%-5.25% | +40%-100% |

### What drives the turnkey premium now
1. **Financing.** Lenders size loans on in-place NOI at a 1.20-1.25x DSCR. Clean buildings get bigger loans.
2. **Insurance.** Carriers price older roofs, electrical and plumbing punitively, or decline them.
3. **Compliance.** SB 721 balcony inspections, and seismic or wiring issues, turn up as due-diligence surprises.
4. **AB 1482 and SB 567 limit the upside.** Renovation evictions are harder, so value-add returns depend on natural turnover.

### So what
- **For a clean listing,** document capex with dates and costs, the SB 721 report, and insurance quotes. That is how you earn the premium.
- **For a value-add listing,** price at a cap rate on in-place income and sell the upside in the story, not in the price.
keyPoints: Turnkey vs. value-add spread: ~50-100 bps of cap rate, or ~10%-20% per unit (estimate)
CBRE Q1 2026 rents: 2010s product $2,890 vs. 1970s product $2,471 (+17%)
New Santal ~$585K/unit vs. older Conejo garden ~$374K/unit
Lenders size on in-place NOI, which favors clean buildings
Document capex, SB 721 compliance and insurability to earn the premium

answers.summary: Buildings with deep below-market rents and long-term tenants trade on in-place NOI, not on the market-rent story. That usually puts them 15%-30% below a stabilized value. Buyers pay a modest premium for upside, because AB 1482 and SB 567 make that upside slow and uncertain.
answers.answer:
### Why the discount exists
- **AB 1482** caps annual increases on most buildings older than 15 years at **5% + CPI, maximum 10%**, and requires just cause for eviction. A unit at $1,800 when market is $2,600 can take years to close the gap.
- **SB 567** (2024) tightened the "substantial remodel" no-fault eviction path, so a buyer cannot quickly turn a building over.
- **City rules** add more limits where they apply. Check each city's current ordinances, including Oxnard's.

### Worked example (10 units, illustrative)
| | In-place | At market |
|---|---|---|
| Avg rent | $1,900 | $2,500 |
| Gross income | $228,000 | $300,000 |
| Expenses (~$91K) | $91,200 | $91,200 |
| NOI | $136,800 | $208,800 |
| Value at 5.25% | **$2.61M** | **$3.98M** |

The roughly $1.37M gap is the **"loss to lease" value**. Buyers typically pay for in-place income at a slightly lower cap, around 5.0%, which works out to about **$2.74M**. That captures only a fraction of the upside. The discount relative to stabilized value is about 30%.

### Long-term tenants specifically
- Turnover in rent-capped units is low, so buyers model about **5%-10% annual turnover** for those units (estimate).
- Elderly or long-tenured tenants raise relocation and reputational risk.
- Buyers will ask for estoppels and an analysis of rent increase history. Missed AB 1482 increases cannot be recaptured.

### How to market it
1. Show a **unit-by-unit rent roll with tenure** and the gap to market for each unit.
2. **Model the realistic path to market:** AB 1482 increases plus turnover, not an instant mark-to-market.
3. **Target the right buyer:** long-hold private capital and 1031 buyers who want stability, not value-add funds on 3-5 year timelines.
4. **If the seller has time,** implement the allowable annual increases before listing, because every dollar of NOI is worth about 19-20x at a 5%-5.25% cap.
keyPoints: Price on in-place NOI; the upside earns only a modest premium
AB 1482: increases capped at 5% + CPI, max 10%, plus just cause
SB 567 (2024) narrowed renovation (substantial remodel) evictions
Typical discount to stabilized value for deeply under-rented buildings: ~15%-30% (estimate)
Each $1 of added NOI is worth ~$19-20 of value at a 5%-5.25% cap

answers.summary: 2-4 unit buildings are priced like houses. Owner-occupant buyers can use residential loans, so caps often run 3.75%-4.75% and GRMs are high. 5+ unit buildings are priced on NOI and commercial debt, around 5.0%-5.5% caps, and draw a smaller, more yield-driven pool of investors.
answers.answer:
### The two markets
| | 2-4 units | 5+ units |
|---|---|---|
| Financing | Residential: 30-year fixed, conforming or FHA/VA if owner-occupied | Commercial: 5-10 year fixed or hybrid, 25-30 year amortization |
| Loan sizing | Borrower income and credit plus property rent | Property NOI, typically 1.20-1.25x DSCR and ~55%-65% LTV |
| Pricing basis | Comps and replacement cost per door | Cap rate on in-place NOI |
| Typical buyer | Owner-occupants, house-hackers, first-time investors | Private investors, 1031 exchangers, family offices, funds |
| Typical cap | ~3.75%-4.75% (est.) | ~5.0%-5.5% (Matthews H1 2026 average 5.37%) |

### Local evidence
- A **Camarillo fourplex at 1917 Colonia Pl** sold for $1,455,000 in H1 2026, about **$364K per unit**.
- Q2 2026 smaller-asset trades averaged about **$270K per unit** (Matthews).
- The fourplex therefore commanded about a 35% per-door premium.

### Why appetite differs right now
- **Residential rates sit below commercial bridge debt,** and owner-occupants accept low or negative cash flow because they are also buying a home.
- **5+ buyers need yield near their cost of debt.** Colliers put permanent debt at 5.5%-6.25% in mid-2026, which keeps their bids disciplined.
- **The 5+ buyer pool is smaller,** so DOM is longer and price reductions are more common (see Q63-Q64).

### So what
- **Selling a 4-plex:** market it through the MLS to owner-users, with residential-style photos and FHA-friendly terms.
- **Selling 5-10 units:** you will usually lose the owner-occupant buyer and face investor underwriting. A 5-unit building can be worth less per door than a 4-plex next door.
- **1031 buyers trading up** from 2-4 units into 5+ are a reliable buyer pool for 5-20 unit listings.
keyPoints: 2-4 units: residential financing and owner-occupant buyers, priced like homes
5+ units: priced on NOI, commercial loans sized at ~1.20-1.25x DSCR
Camarillo 4-plex at ~$364K/unit vs. ~$270K/unit average for small 5+ trades (Q2 2026)
A 5-unit building can be worth less per door than a 4-plex

answers.summary: Off-market deals in Ventura County usually trade at or slightly below where a fully marketed deal would. The seller gives up competitive tension in exchange for certainty, privacy and speed. There are exceptions: the Vines at RiverPark set a county record off-market at about $567K per unit in 2022.
answers.answer:
### General pattern
- **Marketed deals** create competition through a call-for-offers process. That usually produces the best price and terms, especially for clean, well-located assets.
- **Off-market deals** typically clear **0%-5% below** what a marketed process would achieve (estimate). In return, the seller gets:
  - **Certainty and speed:** a known buyer, often 1031 or all-cash
  - **Privacy:** tenants, staff and family don't learn about the sale
  - **Lower friction:** fewer re-trades and no exposure as a stale listing if the deal fails

### Local examples
- **The Vines at RiverPark, Oxnard (2022):** sold **off-market for $93M**, more than $567K per unit and $414/SF. Interstate Equities bought it from Champion Real Estate, with Berkadia advising the seller. A strong off-market price is possible when a motivated buyer pre-empts a process.
- **Alturas, Oxnard (2021):** CGI+ bought it off-market for $50.7M, about $300K per unit, from FPA Multifamily. FPA had paid $34M in 2018.
- In the MLS data, sold multifamily listings with **1-3 days on market** are usually deals arranged before or outside the MLS (see Q64).

### When off-market makes sense for a seller
1. A known buyer at or near the target price, especially one up against a 1031 deadline
2. Sensitive situations: estate, partnership disputes, long-term tenants
3. Small buildings where a marketed process would not attract many more bidders

### When to push for full marketing
1. A clean, institutional-quality or rare asset, such as Conejo Valley or beach-adjacent Ventura
2. A seller who is price-maximizing and has time
3. Multiple likely buyer types, such as 1031, local private and funds

### So what
- **Offer both.** Run a quiet "pocket" test with 10-20 qualified buyers first, then go to full market if the price isn't there.
- **Document the strategy in writing** to protect your fiduciary position.
keyPoints: Off-market typically clears ~0%-5% below a marketed process (estimate)
Sellers trade price for certainty, speed and privacy
Vines at RiverPark: $93M off-market (2022), >$567K/unit, a county record at the time
Alturas, Oxnard: $50.7M off-market (2021), ~$300K/unit
Best practice: a quiet pocket test, then full marketing if the price isn't there

Our working estimate is that about 20%-35% are true off-market or pocket deals. Most of the rest are marketed by investment brokers on CoStar/LoopNet, Crexi or private email lists.
answers.answer:
### What the data hints at
- **MLS:** Flexmls recorded only **11 multifamily closings in Ventura County** in the 12 months to September 2026.
- **Broker-tracked trades:** Matthews counted **11 trades in H1 2026 alone** (about $199M). Matthews counted 26 sales in 2023, and other trackers record more. Most institutional deals (Tempo, Cypress Point, Santal, Allure) were run by JLL, IPA or Newmark through their own processes, not the MLS.

### Rough breakdown (estimated)
| Channel | Share of 5+ unit sales |
|---|---|
| Marketed by investment brokers (OM, CoStar/LoopNet, Crexi, email blasts), not MLS | ~40%-55% |
| Listed on MLS (often cross-listed with LoopNet) | ~15%-25% |
| True off-market or pocket (no broad marketing) | ~20%-35% |

For 2-4 unit properties the MLS share is far higher, since that segment is largely residential.

### Why the off-market share stays meaningful here
- **A small owner base with long holds.** Many owners are approached directly by buyers or brokers they know.
- **1031 buyers** often pre-empt with clean offers.
- **Deals reported as off-market** include the Vines ($93M, 2022) and Alturas ($50.7M, 2021).

### So what
- **Being on the MLS alone misses most of the market.** Get CoStar and Crexi comps and build your own owner database.
- **Off-market deal flow comes from relationships.** That is why direct owner outreach (Section 7) pays off.

answers.summary: Base case for the next 12 months: values flat to +3%, cap rates holding around 5.0%-5.5%, and modestly higher volume. Supply has dropped sharply, occupancy is about 96%, and rent growth is about 1%. The swing factor is the 10-year Treasury.
answers.answer:
### Fundamentals (as of mid-2026)
- **Supply is drying up.** Matthews counts **502 units under construction, 1.3% of inventory**, vs. 2.7% nationally. CBRE recorded **zero completions in Q2 2026** after 585 in Q1.
- **Occupancy is tight.** CBRE reports **96.1%** in Q2 2026. Matthews reports vacancy of **4.2%, down 60 bps** year over year, and expects it to stay stable through 2026.
- **Rent growth is soft but positive.** About **+1.2% year over year** (Matthews), with an average of **$2,769** (CBRE Q2 2026). NAI flagged rising vacant units in late 2025 while new supply leased up.

### Capital markets
- **Rates:** The 10-year Treasury was at 4.4%-4.7% and permanent debt at 5.5%-6.25% in mid-2026 (Colliers). Caps sit roughly at the cost of debt.
- **Survey sentiment:** CBRE's H1 2026 survey found caps flat nationally, with **infill multifamily drawing the most bearish outlook**.
- **Buyers are active:** BlackRock bought unleveraged, and Hines, Raintree and Jackson Square all bought in the past 12 months.

### Scenarios (12 months, illustrative)
| Scenario | 10-yr Treasury | Cap rates | Values |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | Below 4.0% | -25 bps | +5%-8% |
| Base | 4.0%-4.75% | Flat | Flat to +3% (NOI growth) |
| Bear | Above 5.0% | +25-50 bps | -5% to -10% |

### Drivers to watch
1. Treasury yields and lender spreads
2. Absorption of the remaining 2025-2026 deliveries in Camarillo, Oxnard and Simi Valley
3. Insurance and property tax growth
4. State and local rent and eviction rules
5. Local economy, including Naval Base Ventura County, Amgen (Matthews notes its $600M R&D expansion) and agriculture

### So what
- **Low new supply is the long-term bull case.** Ventura is hard to build in.
- **Tell sellers waiting for 2021 pricing that it is not coming back.** Their real choice is between selling at today's 5%-5.5% caps or holding for NOI growth.
